meta.title: Who really said "In the woods, we return to reason and faith"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine. Emerson wrote it in Chapter I of Nature, published anonymously in Boston in 1836, just before the famous transparent eye-ball passage.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In the woods, we return to reason and faith'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Emerson — Nature, Chapter I, Boston 1836. Verified against the first edition and the 1849 revision. The comma after 'woods' is his.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1803–1882 · American essayist, lecturer & poet; founder of Transcendentalism
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and pinnable to the page. The sentence appears in Chapter I of Nature, the essay Emerson sent anonymously to James Munroe and Company in Boston and which was published on 9 September 1836 ↗. It sits two sentences before the famous “transparent eye-ball” passage, and survives unchanged into the 1849 revised edition.

source.heading: The source, confirmed

docMeta.dd: 9 September 1836, anonymously, by James Munroe and Company, Boston
Nature, New Edition (Munroe, 1849) — this sentence unchanged; surrounding paragraph lightly revised

source.excerpt: In the woods too, a man casts off his years, as the snake his slough, and at what period soever of life, is always a child. In the woods, is perpetual youth. Within these plantations of God, a decorum and sanctity reign, a perennial festival is dressed, and the guest sees not how he should tire of them in a thousand years. In the woods, we return to reason and faith. There I feel that nothing can befal me in life,—no disgrace, no calamity, (leaving me my eyes,) which nature cannot repair. Standing on the bare ground,—my head bathed by the blithe air, and uplifted into infinite space,—all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eye-ball. I am nothing. I see all. The currents of the Universal Being circulate through me; I am part or particle of God.
trail: The Wikisource transcription of the 1836 first edition ↗ (Boston: James Munroe and Company) carries the sentence verbatim, comma included, in Chapter I.
Project Gutenberg’s text of the revised 1849 New Edition ↗ reproduces the same paragraph, confirming Emerson kept the line through his own revision.
Wikiquote’s sourced section for Emerson ↗ attributes the immediately following “transparent eye-ball” sentence to Nature (1836); the line appears in no misattributed or disputed list.
Wikipedia records that Emerson sent the essay anonymously to James Munroe and Company for publication on 9 September 1836 ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1836 first edition, which spells it “befal” and ends the eye-ball clauses with full stops. The 1849 revision reads “befall” and uses semicolons; the quoted sentence itself is identical in both.

author.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.heading: Who was Ralph Waldo Emerson?
author.metaLine: 1803–1882 · American essayist, lecturer & poet; founder of Transcendentalism
author.bio: Emerson was a Boston minister who resigned his pulpit at the Second Church in 1832 after concluding he could no longer administer Communion, and spent the rest of his life arguing the same case from the lecture platform instead. Nature, sent anonymously to his publisher in 1836, was the essay that gave the Transcendentalist circle its founding text — a claim that the natural world, not inherited doctrine, is the direct route to the divine. He remains one of the most quoted Americans who ever lived, which is exactly why so many lines he never wrote get pinned to his name.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The citation usually is not.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare Emerson lines that is genuinely Emerson — the attribution survives scrutiny. What does not survive is the paperwork around it. Quote sites route the sentence through modern reprints and anthologies rather than the 1836 essay, and most of them lose a comma on the way.

items.why: AZQuotes prints the line and cites “Emerson: Selected Essays”, p.30, Penguin (1982) ↗ — a twentieth-century selection, not the work the sentence was written for. The original is Nature, Boston: James Munroe and Company, 1836.

LibQuotes attributes the fuller passage to “Nature: An Essay; And, Lectures on the Times” (ed. 1844) ↗, and Goodreads simply files it under “Essays and Poems” ↗. Both are later gatherings of an essay that had already been in print for years.

items.who: “In the woods we return to reason and faith”
items.why: The comma-free version is the one that dominates quote sites and merchandise. Emerson punctuated it — “In the woods, we return to reason and faith.” — in the 1836 first edition ↗ and again in the 1849 revision ↗.

When the sentence is quoted with its neighbours, the version circulating is almost always the 1849 text. The 1836 first edition ↗ reads “nothing can befal me” and separates the eye-ball clauses with full stops rather than semicolons.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Emerson’s own, in Chapter I of Nature — Boston: James Munroe and Company, 1836 ↗. Cite that, keep the comma, and you are quoting him exactly.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Emerson had walked away from the ministry in 1832 because he could not go on serving Communion in good conscience. Nature is what he built in its place: an argument that you do not need a church to reach the divine, because the woods will do it faster. The sentence about reason and faith is the hinge — it borrows the vocabulary of the pulpit and quietly relocates it outdoors.

What follows it in the same paragraph is the strangest image in American letters, and the reason the passage is taught at all: Emerson standing on bare ground, dissolving into pure perception. Contemporaries found it ridiculous enough that the artist Christopher Pearse Cranch drew a cartoon of a literal eyeball on legs. The essay still became the founding document of Transcendentalism, and Thoreau read it as a Harvard student.
context.detailsSummary: The two editions, and which one you are reading
detailsBody: Emerson revised Nature for the 1849 New Edition, and the paragraph carries small but visible marks of the pass. The 1836 first edition reads “nothing can befal me in life” and breaks the eye-ball sentence into flat declaratives separated by full stops. The 1849 text reads “befall” and strings the same clauses together with semicolons.

Nearly every version circulating online is the 1849 text, which is a perfectly legitimate Emerson but is not the 1836 original. The sentence quoted here — “In the woods, we return to reason and faith.” — is identical in both, comma included.
